newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS- Brazil postpones Vale sell-off.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS- Brazil postpones Vale sell-off.

text.p: Political expediency and time constraints may have combined to trigger a one-month delay in the privatization of Brazilian mining giant Vale do Rio Doce, originally scheduled to begin in February.

On Wednesday a spokesman for the Planning Ministry confirmed the Vale sale would probably not take place before March adding that the government's commitment was to privatize the company before the end of the first quarter of 1997.

That announcement comes after National Development Bank (BNDES), the government agency responsible for Brazil's privatization program, said investors were requesting a longer period to study the company before putting their bids together.
With combine assets valued at over $8 billion, Vale is the world's biggest iron ore exporter and its sale will be Latin America's biggest privatization so far.

Analysts said the investors' calls for more time to study the company had served as the perfect excuse for President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to push back Vale's privatization date at a time in which the Vale sale was generating increasing resistance in Congress.

They said the president was concerned the controversy surrounding the Vale sale might emerge as an obstacle to his bid to obtain a constitutional amendment that would allow him to run for a second term in office.
The easiest alternative -- they said -- was to delay the Vale privatization until the re-election debate was over.
"(The government) has managed to combine what is practial with what is convenient," said Marcelo Mesquita, a stock analyst at Banco Garantia.
Analysts said it was natural that there should be delays in the Vale privatization process considering the volume of the assets being put on the block.
They said the postponement should not be interpreted as a sign Cardoso had cooled to the idea of selling off the massive mining company.
On the contrary, it was a sign the government was determined to go ahead with the project despite the opposition of senior politicians, including former presidents Jose Sarney and Itamar Franco.
"We have never sold off anything quite as big as Vale. I think it is normal that there should be delays," said Jose Monforte, Capital Markets director vice-president at Citibank do Brasil.
Analysts said they would not be surprised if the government announced major alternations to the Vale privatization model thus triggering further postponements of the sale date.

Just this week Cardoso said he would consider a proposal put forward by the influential Lower House president Luiz Eduardo Magalhaes in which argued in favor changing the privatization model so as to make available more shares to the public.
"I wouldn't be surprised if the sale didn't take place until April or May," said Mesquita of Banco Garantia. "That's fine by me -- what is important is that it should be privatized."
